name: Greater celandine (Chelidonium majus)
short: Liver injury: acute hepatitis, often with jaundice, in case reports and series (a review counted 38), incl. combination products; recurred on re-exposure. One haemolytic anaemia needing dialysis.
text: This entry covers greater celandine (Chelidonium majus) taken by mouth (extracts, capsules, tea, tinctures and herbal preparations that contain it). Lesser celandine (Ranunculus ficaria) is a different plant; a case report describes acute hepatitis with jaundice in a 36-year-old woman after about 10 days of lesser celandine extract for haemorrhoids, with probable causality on a standard scale. Liver injury: a 2024 report of two cases with a literature review found 38 published cases of herb-induced liver injury with greater celandine preparations, mainly in adult women aged 27 to 77 and mostly reported from Germany; various forms were used, for 1 week to a year, and recovery generally followed stopping. Its two cases were women of 64 and 66, one taking capsules (with transaminases above 1000 IU/L) and one drinking the tea regularly. In a series of 10 people with acute hepatitis from greater celandine preparations, which the authors say are frequently prescribed for gastric and biliary disorders, the course was mild to severe and marked cholestasis occurred in 5, but none had liver failure; all recovered after stopping, with liver tests normal in 2 to 6 months, and one had a second flare after taking it again unintentionally. A clinical review of 16 patients from several European countries found jaundice with high liver enzymes in virtually all, with a favourable outcome despite a severe course. Other case reports describe acute liver injury in two people taking greater celandine, which the authors call a remedy frequently used for irritable bowel syndrome (cholestatic hepatitis recurred rapidly in one after re-exposure), severe acute cholestatic hepatitis in a 58-year-old man, and acute hepatitis with jaundice and centrilobular necrosis on biopsy in a 60-year-old woman, all of whom improved after stopping; another report describes acute hepatitis in a 72-year-old US man taking it for nausea (the abstract does not give the outcome). Strength of the link: a reanalysis of 21 published cases with a liver-specific scale rated the link highly probable in 2, probable in 6, possible in 10 and excluded in 3, with confounding and poor data quality lowering some ratings; an analysis of 22 spontaneous reports from Germany rated it highly probable in 2, probable in 6, possible in 10, unlikely in 1 and excluded in 3 (mean age 56.4 years, mean treatment 36.4 days, female predominance), and says the link is less strong than had been assumed. A review of herb-induced liver injury cases with positive re-exposure tests lists greater celandine among herbs whose liver-injury potential was confirmed this way. A 2017 review concludes that the risk-to-benefit ratio of products containing greater celandine can be considered negative. Combination preparations: acute hepatitis with jaundice developed in a 42-year-old woman several weeks after a preparation of greater celandine with curcuma root, with recovery within 2 months of stopping; and acute severe hepatitis with jaundice developed in a 32-year-old woman taking a nine-herb preparation that includes greater celandine, resolving 5 weeks after stopping, with the authors noting occasional earlier cases of liver injury with that preparation. Other harms: a 1990 case report describes haemolytic anaemia after an oral greater celandine extract, with kidney failure needing dialysis twice, liver cell injury and low platelets, resolving by about day 12. In contrast, a case series of 20 outpatients with COVID-19 treated with a greater celandine mother tincture for 3 to 12 days reported no adverse events. None of the cited abstracts reports a death or a liver transplant. The cited sources give no data on pregnancy; the COVID-19 series included patients aged 14 to 71, and no other cited source reports on children. Interactions (laboratory data only): chelidonine, a major constituent of greater celandine, inactivated the human drug-metabolising enzyme CYP2D6 in laboratory tests, and the authors say this may lead to drug interactions; no study in people was found.
